## Numbrino (Cocaine HCl 4% Nasal Solution)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/numbrino/
- aliases: Numbrino, Cocaine nasal solution, Cocaine hydrochloride spray, Legal cocaine
- category: Stimulants
- schedule: Schedule II (US) — approved pharmaceutical; dispensed to clinics/hospitals, not to patients
- appearance: Single-use 4 mL bottles of 4% (40 mg/mL) clear solution, NDC 0527-1961; box labeled 'FOR TOPICAL USE ONLY. NOT FOR INJECTION OR OPHTHALMIC USE'
- effects: Local anesthesia of the nasal mucosa plus vasoconstriction — numbs the nose and stops bleeding during ENT procedures; Applied by a clinician on soaked cotton/pads or sprayed; patients are monitored
- risks: IT'S NOT PRESCRIBED LIKE NORMAL MEDICINE: Numbrino is ordered by hospitals and ENT clinics as a procedure supply — there is no take-home prescription pathway for patients. Anyone 'selling Numbrino online' is selling diverted pharmaceutical stock or counterfeits — a federal felony; Systemic absorption is real even topically: cardiovascular strain, blood pressure spikes, possible arrhythmia; Label warnings: seizure risk, not for patients with epilepsy/cardiovascular disease; NOT for injection or eye use; Same addiction pharmacology as street cocaine if misused — the Schedule II classification exists because of it; Diversion from clinics is rare but documented historically with medical cocaine
- overdoseSigns: (Clinical misuse) chest pain, racing irregular heart; Severe agitation, seizures; Hypertensive crisis signs
- streetPrice: Not a street product; any 'for sale' listing online ($100–$300/bottle claims) is diversion or counterfeit
- legalStatus: FDA-approved December 2019 (Lannett) for anesthesia of the nasal mucosa in adults — an in-clinic pharmaceutical. Schedule II. Personal possession without legitimate medical context is treated like any other cocaine offense.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-21
- sources: FDA, DEA, Lannett prescribing information

## Ketamine Nasal Spray (Gray-Market & Compounded)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/ketamine-nasal-spray/
- aliases: K nasal spray, Ketamine spray, Compounded ketamine, Special K spray, At-home Spravato
- category: Dissociatives
- schedule: Spravato (esketamine) = Schedule III, REMS clinic-only; compounded/gray sprays unregulated
- appearance: Small spray bottles of clear liquid sold online as 'ketamine nasal spray' or 'K spray'; compounded versions from telehealth clinics; distinct from Spravato's clinic-administered device
- effects: Dissociation, euphoria, calm — onset 5–15 min via nasal route; Marketed for 'depression treatment at home' by telehealth clinics and grey sellers
- risks: THE DOSAGE LIE: grey-market sprays rarely state mg/mL accurately — a 'spray' can be anything from a threshold dose to a k-hole; bottles from the same seller vary; Bladder damage (ketamine cystitis) risk identical to powder — daily spray use makes it easy to use daily; Dependence creeps fastest with convenient formats; the spray removes every friction point; Telehealth 'ketamine at home' prescribing has drawn FDA scrutiny and state crackdowns (2024–2025) after adverse events; Never drive — impairment from a nasal dose lasts 1–3 hours; Spravato exists ONLY as a clinic-locked REMS program for one reason: monitoring. Any 'at-home Spravato' is a red flag
- overdoseSigns: Heavy dissociative sedation, unresponsive but eyes open; Vomiting while impaired; Slow breathing (rare alone; dangerous with depressants)
- streetPrice: Grey sprays $60–$150 per bottle; telehealth programs $200–$600/mo; Spravato clinic course $4,700+/mo
- legalStatus: Esketamine (Spravato) Rx + REMS-locked; compounded ketamine in a legal gray zone being tightened; gray-market sprays illegal everywhere
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-21
- sources: FDA, DEA, EMA, NIDA

## Bromazolam
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/bromazolam/
- aliases: Bromo, Bromaz, Fake Xanax, Designer Xanax
- category: Benzodiazepines
- schedule: Not federally scheduled (US) as of 2026 — several US states emergency-scheduled; controlled in multiple EU countries and the UK
- appearance: White to off-white powder, pressed into counterfeit Xanax/Valium bars or sold as pellets; active at 1–3 mg
- effects: Sedation, anxiety relief and muscle relaxation — like alprazolam but often stronger per milligram; Short-term memory loss and blackouts, especially above ~3 mg; Compulsive redosing when the blackout makes you forget you already took some
- risks: The #1 novel benzodiazepine detected in counterfeit 'Xanax bars' in North America since 2023 — most users have no idea they're taking it; Pressed bars have wildly uneven doses: one quarter of a bar can floor you while the next does nothing; Multi-day blackouts, falls, car accidents and assault risk; Dependence within weeks; withdrawal can cause seizures and kills faster than opioid withdrawal; Frequently found together with fentanyl in the same supply — respiratory depression stacks
- overdoseSigns: Unrousable sleep that outlasts a normal dose by many hours; Very slow or irregular breathing, especially mixed with opioids; Cold, clammy skin; gurgling or snoring breath sounds
- streetPrice: ~$2–$5 per pressed 'bar'; ~$30–$80/g powder
- legalStatus: Unscheduled federally in the US (state bans spreading); Class C-style controls in UK; controlled in DE/SE and others; analogue prosecutions possible
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-21
- sources: DEA, CFSRE, CDC, Aegis, UNODC

## Medetomidine
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/medetomidine/
- aliases: Medeto, New tranq, Medetomidine dope
- category: Opioids
- schedule: Not federally scheduled (US) as of 2026; veterinary anesthetic, no approved human use
- appearance: No street form of its own — detected as a whitish powder mixed into fentanyl/heroin, often alongside xylazine and BTMPS
- effects: Profound, hours-long sedation and blackout; Very slow heart rate and breathing; severe drops in blood pressure; In someone opioid-dependent: precipitated, violent withdrawal on top of opioid withdrawal
- risks: Not an opioid — naloxone does NOT reverse it, and it still shuts down breathing; The successor to xylazine: detected in 18+ US states and roughly a third of tested opioid samples by late 2025; Withdrawal is ICU-grade — severe hypertension, racing heart, agitation — and standard opioid-withdrawal treatment (clonidine protocols) often fails; Wounds and tissue damage like xylazine's are being reported
- overdoseSigns: Unresponsive with slow or gasping breathing; Pinpoint pupils plus bradycardia (slow pulse) — a mixed picture that confuses responders; Blue-gray lips and extremities
- streetPrice: Sold as part of fentanyl/heroin bags (~$10–$40) — no separate price
- legalStatus: Veterinary Rx-only; human use illegal; treated as an adulterant in prosecutions, often charged by total mixture weight
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-21
- sources: CDC, DEA, CFSRE, JAMA

## 7-Hydroxymitragynine (7-OH)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/7-hydroxymitragynine/
- aliases: 7-OH, 7-hydroxy, Concentrated kratom, Tabz, 7-OH shots
- category: Opioids
- schedule: FDA recommended Schedule I (July 2025); DEA issued Notices of Intent to temporarily schedule 7-OH + 3 synthetic derivatives (July 2026); banned or restricted in several US states
- appearance: Tablets, pellets, gummies and concentrated 'shots' sold at gas stations, vape shops and online — far stronger than kratom leaf per dose
- effects: Opioid-like analgesia and warmth at low doses; Euphoria and heavy sedation at higher doses; Onset within minutes for shots/tablets — much faster than kratom tea
- risks: Dependence forms fast — often within 1–2 weeks of daily use; Withdrawal is opioid-type (restless legs, cramps, insomnia, diarrhea) and can be severe; users report it's harder to quit than kratom leaf; Respiratory depression, especially mixed with alcohol, benzos or other opioids; Seizures reported; rare liver injury; Products are unregulated — labeled strengths routinely fail third-party testing, sometimes by a factor of 10
- overdoseSigns: Pinpoint pupils; Slow, shallow breathing; gurgling sounds; Unresponsiveness; blue lips or fingertips
- streetPrice: ~$10–$40 per bottle of shots or pack of tablets
- legalStatus: Federal scheduling in progress (DEA NOI July 2026); already banned/restricted in states including FL and TN; FDA seizures ongoing
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-21
- sources: FDA, DEA, CDC, NIDA

## Phencyclidine (PCP)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/pcp/
- aliases: Angel dust, Sherm, Shermans, Dipper, Wet, Embalming fluid, Rocket fuel
- category: Dissociatives
- schedule: Schedule II (US); Class A (UK); controlled virtually everywhere
- appearance: White crystalline powder, clear yellowish liquid, or cigarettes/blunts dipped in liquid PCP ('sherms', 'dippers')
- effects: Strong dissociation — feeling detached from your body; numbness; Euphoria, bursts of energy, distorted body image and hallucinations; Horizontal or vertical eye jerks (nystagmus) — a clinical tell; Effects last 4–8 hours; residual fogginess for a day or more
- risks: Acute behavioral toxicity: panic, paranoia and unpredictable aggression, worsened in unfamiliar or stressful settings; Rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown) from struggling/restraint → kidney failure; Dangerously high blood pressure, seizures, hyperthermia; Long-term use: memory loss, speech problems, persistent psychosis, depression and suicidal thinking; Mixing with alcohol or benzos compounds sedation; with stimulants, blood pressure can become lethal
- overdoseSigns: Severe agitation or catatonic stillness alternating; Fever with rigid muscles and seizures; Very high blood pressure; coma in severe cases
- streetPrice: ~$5–$30 per dipped cigarette; ~$50–$100/g powder
- legalStatus: Schedule II (US); Class A (UK); Schedule I-class controls across EU; veterinary (ketamine) analogues separately controlled
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-21
- sources: NIDA, DEA, EMCDDA, UNODC

## Crack Cocaine
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/crack/
- aliases: Crack, Rock, Stones, Base, Freebase
- category: Stimulants
- schedule: Schedule II (US); Class A (UK); criminalized everywhere we track
- appearance: Small off-white to beige 'rocks' that smoke with a crackling sound — smoked in glass pipes, sometimes with steel wool or brillo
- effects: Intense but very short euphoria (5–15 minutes), energy and confidence; Rapid crash: irritability, exhaustion, intense craving for another hit; Smoked route hits the brain in seconds — one of the most reinforcing drug experiences known
- risks: The short high creates a compulsive redosing loop that drives binge patterns and rapid dependence; Crack lung: chest pain, cough and lung bleeding (eosinophilic pneumonitis) after smoking sessions; Chipped/burned lips and pipe-sharing spread MRSA, hepatitis C and other infections; Heart attack, dangerous arrhythmias and stroke — risk is real even in young users; Paranoia, aggression and stimulant psychosis with binges; malnutrition and sleep loss compound harm; Same supply risk as powder cocaine: cuts and, increasingly, fentanyl contamination
- overdoseSigns: Chest pain, pounding or irregular heartbeat; Seizures; extremely high body temperature; Severe agitation, paranoia or hallucinations; Stroke signs: one-sided weakness, slurred speech, facial droop
- streetPrice: ~$10–$20 per rock; quantity discounts on the gram
- legalStatus: Schedule II (US); Class A (UK); penalties typically track powder cocaine with small quantity distinctions in some jurisdictions
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-21
- sources: NIDA, DEA, CDC, EMCDDA

## DMAA
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/dmaa/
- aliases: 1,3-DMAA, Geranium extract, Methylhexanamine, Geranamine
- category: Stimulants
- schedule: Not a legal dietary ingredient (US FDA 2013); controlled in several countries including Australia, Canada, Brazil
- appearance: White crystalline powder; typical pre-workout dose 25–75 mg
- effects: Sharp, tunnel-vision energy and focus at 25–50 mg; Elevated heart rate and blood pressure — the 'cracked-out' workout feel; Crash and irritability as it wears off (~2–4 h)
- risks: Linked to deaths, hemorrhagic strokes and cardiac events; FDA issued warning letters from 2012 and ruled it an adulterant in 2013; Blood pressure and heart-rate spikes dangerous for anyone with cardiac risk; Sold for years as 'geranium extract' despite containing no detectable DMAA from natural sources; Banned from competition by WADA and most sports federations
- overdoseSigns: Chest pain, severe headache, pounding or irregular heartbeat; Spiking blood pressure, confusion, collapse; Stroke symptoms: one-sided weakness, slurred speech
- streetPrice: ~$1–3 per dose inside pre-workout tubs ($30–60 per bottle); gray-market powder ~$20–40/g
- legalStatus: FDA: not a lawful supplement ingredient; products containing it are adulterated. Scheduled in AU/CA/BR and others. Gray zone persists in some markets.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-21
- sources: FDA, WADA, regulatory alerts

## DMHA
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/dmha/
- aliases: 2-Aminoisoheptane, Octodrine, Juglans regia extract, Aminoisoheptane
- category: Stimulants
- schedule: Unscheduled federally (US) but FDA has warned; controlled in Australia and several other countries
- appearance: White-to-off-white powder in pre-workout and fat-burner products; typical dose 100–200 mg
- effects: Stimulating, appetite-suppressing energy similar to DMAA but usually milder and shorter; Elevated heart rate, blood pressure and body temperature; Insomnia and anxiety at high doses
- risks: Successor to DMAA in the same cat-and-mouse pattern: launched as 'geranium/juglans extract' shortly after DMAA was banned; Human safety data essentially absent — structure predicts similar cardiovascular stress to DMAA; Frequently combined with extreme caffeine stacks that multiply cardiac load; WADA-banned in competition
- overdoseSigns: Racing or irregular heartbeat, chest pressure; Severe anxiety, tremor, overheating; Fainting or collapse during exercise
- streetPrice: ~$1–3 per dose inside pre-workout tubs; gray-market bulk powder widely available
- legalStatus: US: unscheduled but FDA warning letters issued; 'not a dietary ingredient' enforcement risk. Scheduled in AU and others. Status varies by country.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-21
- sources: FDA, WADA, regulatory alerts

## Tirzepatide (Mounjaro / Zepbound)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/tirzepatide/
- aliases: Mounjaro, Zepbound, GIP/GLP-1, Twincretin
- category: Weight Loss & Metabolic Meds
- schedule: Rx-only (US/EU/UK); approved 2022–2023 for diabetes and chronic weight management
- appearance: Single-dose injection pen (2.5–15 mg weekly) for the real drug; grey-market 'research' vials and lyophilized powder for the counterfeits
- effects: Appetite suppression via dual GIP + GLP-1 receptor activation — the strongest weight-loss drug class as of 2026 (trials: ~20% of body weight at the top dose); Slower stomach emptying — early fullness, quieter 'food noise'; Improved blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes
- risks: The #1 target of GLP-1 counterfeiting after semaglutide — fake Mounjaro/Zepbound pens seized across the US, UK and EU with wrong doses, wrong drugs, or bacterial contamination; Compounded and grey-market versions are not interchangeable with the approved pen — dose errors are common; Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are the norm in the first weeks; dehydration follows heavy GI loss; Gallbladder disease, pancreatitis (rare) and muscle loss without adequate protein and resistance training; Weight returns after stopping — this is a long-term medicine, not a course
- overdoseSigns: Severe, unrelenting vomiting or diarrhea leading to dizziness and fainting (dehydration); Severe upper-abdominal pain radiating to the back (pancreatitis — emergency); Confusion and weakness from inability to keep fluids down
- streetPrice: ~$25–60 per weekly pen equivalent on grey markets; counterfeit pens sold at 'discount' prices that undercut pharmacies
- legalStatus: Prescription-only everywhere it's approved; purchasing Rx medicine without a prescription is illegal in the US, UK and EU. Counterfeit pens are criminal-product territory regardless of drug laws.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-22
- sources: FDA, EMA, Novo/Eli Lilly safety communications, DEA counterfeit alerts

## Retatrutide ('Reta')
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/retatrutide/
- aliases: Reta, LY3437943, Triple G, Retatrutide acetate
- category: Weight Loss & Metabolic Meds
- schedule: Investigational — not approved anywhere as of 2026; in Phase 3 trials; grey-market sale is unregulated
- appearance: Grey-market: lyophilized (freeze-dried) powder in vials, sold with bacteriostatic water for self-injection; no legitimate consumer product exists
- effects: Triple agonist (GIP + GLP-1 + glucagon) — trial results through 2025 show weight loss up to ~28–30% of body weight, the largest effect ever recorded for an obesity drug; Strong appetite suppression and altered food preference; Not a finished medicine — everything sold today is experimental powder dosed by guesswork
- risks: The most-searched grey-market peptide of 2025–26 — demand outran the clinical trial program within a year; Zero quality control: vial contents range from underdosed to contaminated; independent tests of grey-market 'reta' have found wrong peptides and endotoxins; Rodent studies of the class flag thyroid C-cell tumors — the human relevance is unknown because the drug is still being studied; Heart-rate increase, GI distress, gallbladder events — monitored in trials, invisible on the grey market; Self-injection without medical supervision: infection, dosing errors, and no one to call when something goes wrong
- overdoseSigns: Persistent vomiting/diarrhea with signs of dehydration; Racing or irregular heartbeat at rest; Lump or hoarseness that persists (thyroid warning sign — see a doctor)
- streetPrice: ~$150–400 per month of grey-market vials; real trial supply is not legally for sale at any price
- legalStatus: Not approved or scheduled — selling it for human use violates drug and pharmacy law in most countries; 'for research purposes only' labels are a legal fig leaf, not a shield.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-22
- sources: Lilly trial publications, FDA, EMCDDA/EUDA NPS monitoring

## Phenazolam (Clobromazolam)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/phenazolam/
- aliases: Clobromazolam, Phenazo, Designer long-tail benzo
- category: Benzodiazepines
- schedule: Not federally scheduled (US) as of 2026 — several EU countries and UK controls; analogue-act prosecutions possible
- appearance: White powder, pressed into counterfeit benzo pills or sold as pellets; active in the ~0.5–1 mg range
- effects: Heavy, long-lasting sedation — clobromazolam is among the most long-acting designer benzos, with effects that can stretch 12+ hours and a half-life measured in days; Strong anxiolysis and muscle relaxation at low doses; Blackout territory above ~1–2 mg, especially combined with other depressants
- risks: Overtaking bromazolam in several European drug-checking and forensic reports — the designer-beno rotation continues one molecule ahead of the law; Extreme duration: redosing before the first dose has peaked stacks sedatives for days; Pressed pills carry uneven doses — one half can floor you while the other does nothing; Dependence forms fast; withdrawal from long-acting benzos is protracted — weeks of anxiety, insomnia and seizure risk; Found alongside opioids in the same supplies — respiratory depression stacks
- overdoseSigns: Unrousable sleep far longer than intended; Very slow or irregular breathing, especially mixed with opioids; Cold, clammy skin; snoring or gurgling breath sounds
- streetPrice: ~$2–5 per pressed pill; ~$40–90/g powder
- legalStatus: Unscheduled federally in the US; controlled in the UK and several EU states; treated as an analogue in prosecutions. State and national scheduling is spreading.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-22
- sources: EUDA drug-checking reports, CFSRE, UNODC, WEDINOS

## Etonitazepyne (NPE)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/etonitazepyne/
- aliases: NPE, Etonitazepyne HCl, 'Neo' nitazene
- category: Opioids
- schedule: Schedule I treatment via analogue enforcement (US); controlled in UK/EU; listed under the 1961 UN Convention scheduling of nitazene class precursors
- appearance: Off-white to yellowish powder, active in the microgram range; pressed into fake oxycodone/hydrocodone pills and mixed into heroin/fentanyl supplies
- effects: Potent nitazene opioid — euphoria, warmth and heavy sedation like other members of the class, at a fraction of the weight; Effects last 4–8 hours, longer than fentanyl — and so does the overdose risk window; Tolerance builds immediately; doses escalate within days
- risks: The leading 'next-generation' nitazene in 2025–26 seizure and toxicology reports — positioned to replace isotonitazene as the class's flagship; Dosed in micrograms: the line between a dose and a fatal overdose is invisible without laboratory equipment; Counterfeit pills containing NPE are sold as 30 mg oxycodone — users have no idea they're taking a drug orders of magnitude stronger; Naloxone still works, but high-potency overdoses often need repeated doses and rescue breathing while it catches up; Dependence and withdrawal hit hard and fast — full opioid dependence within weeks of regular use
- overdoseSigns: Unrousable, blue lips or fingertips; Breathing fewer than 8 times a minute, or not at all; Pinpoint pupils with gurgling or snoring sounds — give naloxone, call emergency services, start rescue breathing
- streetPrice: ~$20–60 per gram wholesale — pennies per lethal dose, which is exactly why it's in the supply
- legalStatus: Effectively Schedule I in the US via the Federal Analogue Act and specific state schedules; Class A (UK); controlled across the EU. Distribution carries fentanyl-analogue-level penalties.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-22
- sources: DEA Emerging Threat reports, EUDA, CFSRE, CDC

## Para-fluorofentanyl (4-FBF)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/para-fluorofentanyl/
- aliases: pFF, 4-FBF, Fluorofentanyl
- category: Opioids
- schedule: Schedule I (US, since 2020s); controlled in Canada, UK, EU
- appearance: White to off-white powder; found loose, in fake oxycodone pills, and mixed into heroin and cocaine supplies
- effects: Fentanyl-family opioid — same warmth, sedation and euphoria, typically described as slightly longer-acting than fentanyl itself; Roughly comparable overdose potency to fentanyl by weight; effects outlast the initial rush; Same instant dependence pattern: tolerance within days, withdrawal within weeks
- risks: The most-reported fentanyl analogue in DEA forensic casework — when a seizure report says 'fentanyl analogue,' this is often the molecule; Presence in cocaine supplies means stimulant users with zero opioid tolerance are overdosing without ever choosing an opioid; Naloxone reverses it, but long-acting analogues can re-sedate after naloxone wears off — stay with the person until help arrives; Pressed 'oxy 30s' containing pFF instead of oxycodone have killed people who thought they were taking a known dose; Same adulterant trajectory: dealers mix it with xylazine, medetomidine and cutting agents like BTMPS
- overdoseSigns: Unrousable, slow or absent breathing; Blue lips or fingertips; cold, clammy skin; Gurgling or snoring sounds — naloxone now, rescue breathing, emergency call
- streetPrice: ~$15–40/g wholesale; fake 'oxy' pills ~$2–5 each
- legalStatus: Schedule I (US); controlled in Canada, UK and EU. Trafficking penalties track fentanyl itself.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-22
- sources: DEA National Forensic Laboratory reports, CDC, EUDA

## BTMPS (Tinuvin 770)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/btmps/
- aliases: Tinuvin 770, HALS-770, Bis(2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-4-piperidyl) sebacate
- category: Hazardous Substances
- schedule: Not a controlled substance — an industrial chemical with no legitimate human use
- appearance: White crystalline granules or powder, sold legitimately as a light stabilizer for plastics and coatings; in drug supplies it's an invisible powder cut into fentanyl
- effects: No psychoactive effects of its own at relevant doses — people take it unknowingly inside fentanyl; Acts as a CYP enzyme inhibitor, slowing the body's breakdown of fentanyl and extending its sedating effects for hours beyond the norm; The result: overdose symptoms that outlast naloxone's window
- risks: Identified in 2024 as the cutting agent behind mass-overdose clusters in the US Midwest — multiple naloxone-resistant-appearing overdoses traced to the same fentanyl batch; The 'no naloxone response' pattern isn't because naloxone fails — it's because the sedative keeps being re-released as the body slowly clears the mix; repeat dosing and rescue breathing are essential; Industrial-grade material carries unknown impurities; chronic effects of inhaling or injecting a plastic stabilizer are unstudied; Its presence is invisible — users can't taste, see or test for it with fentanyl strips; A preview of the future: as cutting agents evolve, overdose clusters will increasingly involve non-opioid chemistry that naloxone can't touch
- overdoseSigns: Sedation that repeatedly returns after naloxone wears off (30–90 minutes) — expect re-dosing; Prolonged unresponsiveness with slow breathing lasting many hours; Clusters of simultaneous overdoses from the same batch — treat as contaminated supply, alert others
- streetPrice: Legitimate industrial chemical ~$5–15/kg — worth pennies per cut dose
- legalStatus: Unscheduled and legal to buy as an industrial chemical; its presence in drug supply is an adulteration issue, not a possession one (though drug delivery charges apply where such laws exist).
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-22
- sources: DEA Emerging Threat reports, CDC Health Alert Network, state poison control bulletins

## O-Desmethyltramadol (O-DSMT)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/o-dsmt/
- aliases: O-DSMT, Desmetramadol, O-DST, The tramadol metabolite
- category: Opioids
- schedule: Not federally scheduled (US) as of 2026 — several countries control it; analogue and Rx-drug-law exposure
- appearance: White crystalline powder, sold online as a 'research chemical'; pressed into pills or dissolved for liquid dosing
- effects: Tramadol's active metabolite, ready-made — the same opioid effect without waiting on your liver's CYP2D6 enzyme; Stronger and more reliable than tramadol: users describe it as roughly oxycodone-adjacent at equivalent doses; Some serotonin/norepinephrine activity carries over — a mild antidepressant-like undertone at low doses
- risks: The most-used research-chemical opioid of 2025–26 — the default pick for people leaving scheduled opioids or priced out of the nitazene market; Predictable by design: unlike tramadol, there is no 'poor metabolizer gets nothing' loophole — every user gets the full opioid load; Dependence arrives on a tramadol schedule: weeks of daily use, then a two-front withdrawal (opioid flu plus serotonin crash); Seizure risk at high doses remains, as does serotonin syndrome when mixed with antidepressants, DXM or MAOIs; Same supply-chain opacity as every RC: independent tests have found mislabeled batches and active-dose swings of 2–3x
- overdoseSigns: Slow or irregular breathing; unrousable sleep; Seizures — convulsions with or without loss of consciousness; Agitation, sweating and diarrhea plus confusion (serotonin syndrome pattern when mixed)
- streetPrice: ~$20–50/g powder; ~$1–3 per 50 mg dose equivalent
- legalStatus: Unscheduled federally (US) as of 2026 but actively monitored; controlled in Sweden, Germany and others. Analogue-act and Rx-drug prosecutions possible; status is tightening.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-22
- sources: EUDA NPS reports, CFSRE, community toxicology reports

## Bupropion (Wellbutrin / Zyban)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/bupropion/
- aliases: Wellbutrin, Zyban, Budeprion, 'Poor man's cocaine'
- category: Stimulants
- schedule: Rx-only (US/UK/EU); unscheduled — one of the most-prescribed antidepressants worldwide
- appearance: 75/100/150/300 mg tablets (immediate and extended release); abused by insufflation or injection of crushed pills
- effects: NDRI antidepressant — norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake blocker; energizing, activating, pro-focus at prescribed doses; Smoking-cessation aid (Zyban) — cuts cravings and withdrawal; At high doses: stimulant-like euphoria, talkativeness and energy — the 'poor man's cocaine' label comes from crushing and snorting 300+ mg
- risks: Seizure risk is dose-dependent and real — crushing XR tablets or exceeding ~450 mg/day sharply raises the odds; injecting dissolved pills is seizure-and-infection roulette; The 'stimulant' effect tempts mixing with alcohol, benzos or opioids — combination queries are enormous because users are trying to chase or soften the edges; Anxiety, insomnia and blood-pressure spikes at recreational doses; the crash includes irritability and low mood; Contraindicated with seizure disorders and eating disorders — recreational dosing ignores both screens; XR tablets are designed to release slowly; defeating the matrix dumps the full daily dose at once
- overdoseSigns: Seizure — the signature bupropion overdose event, can occur hours after ingestion; Hallucinations, agitation, rapid heart rate and high blood pressure; Fever and muscle rigidity in severe toxicity — emergency department territory
- streetPrice: Cheap where diverted: ~$1–5 per 150 mg tablet; 'script mills' and fake online pharmacies sell counterfeit versions with random contents
- legalStatus: Prescription-only; unscheduled. Possession without a prescription is illegal in the US and most countries; sale is pharmacy-law territory, not trafficking — unless counterfeit pills are involved.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-22
- sources: FDA label, poison control data, treatment admissions literature

## SSRIs & SNRIs (the antidepressant class)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/ssris-snris/
- aliases: Fluoxetine, Sertraline, Escitalopram, Paroxetine, Citalopram, Venlafaxine, Duloxetine, Antidepressants
- category: Sedatives & Hypnotics
- schedule: Rx-only; unscheduled — the most-prescribed drug class on earth
- appearance: Daily tablets or capsules (10–100 mg depending on drug); never sold as a 'high' — the misuse angle is entirely about mixing them with everything else
- effects: Lift depression and anxiety by raising serotonin (SSRIs) or serotonin + norepinephrine (SNRIs) over weeks, not hours — no same-day high, no addiction in the classic sense; Take 2–6 weeks to work; missed doses and stopping cause a distinct withdrawal-like 'discontinuation syndrome': brain zaps, dizziness, irritability; Emotional blunting at higher doses is common and under-discussed
- risks: The mainstream class people actually mix with everything — and most of the mixing questions are answered with 'don't': alcohol multiplies sedation and worsens depression; MDMA is blunted AND carries serotonin-syndrome risk; tramadol, DXM, St John's Wort, triptans and MAOIs stack serotonin dangerously; Serotonin syndrome: agitation, sweating, diarrhea, muscle rigidity, fever, confusion — an emergency when severe, and the reason 'can I drink on…' searches matter; SNRIs (especially venlafaxine) have the harshest discontinuation — missing 1–2 doses can cause dizziness and 'brain zaps'; Alcohol + SSRI doesn't poison the liver directly — it deepens sedation, impairs judgment and quietly reverses the medication's benefit; Citalopram/escitalopram carry a dose-dependent heart-rhythm warning — relevant when people double doses carelessly
- overdoseSigns: Serotonin syndrome: agitation, sweating, diarrhea, fever, muscle rigidity — especially after a mix; Seizures after massive single overdoses (rare but documented); Excessive drowsiness with vomiting after mixing with alcohol or sleep meds
- streetPrice: Not a street drug — diverted scripts ~$0.50–2 per tablet; the 'market' is fake online pharmacies and sharing
- legalStatus: Prescription-only worldwide; unscheduled. The danger profile is interaction-driven, not possession-driven.
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-22
- sources: FDA labels, MHRA interaction guidance, toxicology reviews

## Nalmefene (Opvee)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/nalmefene/
- aliases: Opvee, Nalmefene nasal spray, Long-acting Narcan
- category: Opioids
- schedule: Rx-only — not a controlled drug; not abusable
- appearance: 5 mg/0.5 mL single-dose nasal spray (bright blue device); hospital injection
- effects: Long-acting opioid antagonist — kicks opioids off receptors and blocks them for ~11 hours (naloxone lasts 60–90 minutes); No opioid effect of its own; it cannot get you high; Carried by an increasing number of US first-responder agencies since its 2023 FDA approval
- risks: Precipitates sudden, severe withdrawal in opioid-dependent people — vomiting and agitation while semi-sedated is an aspiration risk; Because it outlasts most opioids, re-overdose is less likely than with naloxone — but the withdrawal it triggers can drive immediate re-use once it wears off; Not a substitute for emergency care: anyone reversed still needs monitoring
- overdoseSigns: This IS an overdose antidote — the danger signs belong to the person being reversed: gasping then violent vomiting, chest pain, extreme agitation; If the person re-sedates (rare with nalmefene), call emergency services again
- streetPrice: Not a street drug — dispensed to EMS/ERs and by prescription (~$100–200 per device retail)
- legalStatus: Rx-only; FDA-approved 2023 for known/suspected opioid overdose in adults and pediatrics (≥12)
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA, CDC

## Methocarbamol (Robaxin)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/methocarbamol/
- aliases: Robaxin, Robaxacet, Methocarbamol 500/750
- category: Sedatives & Hypnotics
- schedule: Rx-only — not a controlled substance (some US states watch it)
- appearance: White 500/750 mg tablets; injection in hospitals
- effects: Centrally-acting muscle relaxant — sedation and relief of muscle spasm, not a true 'relaxant' at the muscle itself; Milder and less abusable than carisoprodol (Soma); Commonly combined with ibuprofen or acetaminophen in brand products
- risks: Compounds every CNS depressant: alcohol, opioids, benzos and sleep meds together can slow breathing to dangerous levels; Crushing and injecting tablets causes abscesses, collapsed veins and infection — a documented jail/practice; Can cause extreme sedation and confusion in older adults (falls, delirium)
- overdoseSigns: Extreme drowsiness, slow breathing, seizures (rare), low blood pressure; Bluish lips, unresponsiveness — call emergency services
- streetPrice: ~$0.50–2 per tablet; near-worthless as a street drug
- legalStatus: Rx-only; not federally controlled
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA, PubMed

## Tizanidine (Zanaflex)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/tizanidine/
- aliases: Zanaflex, Tizan, 4 mg muscle relaxer
- category: Sedatives & Hypnotics
- schedule: Rx-only — not a controlled substance
- appearance: White/colored 2–4 mg tablets and capsules; bitter taste
- effects: Alpha-2 agonist muscle relaxant — reduces spasticity; causes real sedation and lowers blood pressure; Short-acting (3–6 hours), so it is dosed up to 3× daily; Same drug family as clonidine — which is why it feels like a blood-pressure pill, not a 'high'
- risks: First doses can crash blood pressure — fainting, falls, especially when standing; Liver injury (rare but real); dangerous with alcohol, opioids or benzos; STOPPING ABRUPTLY after regular use causes rebound hypertension and racing heart — taper under medical care
- overdoseSigns: Fainting, very slow heart rate, severe drowsiness, shallow breathing (worse mixed with other depressants); Unresponsive — call emergency services
- streetPrice: ~$0.50–2 per tablet; occasional misuse as a sedative or opioid potentiator
- legalStatus: Rx-only; not federally controlled
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA, PubMed

## Amitriptyline & Tricyclics (Elavil)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/amitriptyline/
- aliases: Elavil, Amitriptyline 10/25/50, TCA, Nortriptyline (cousin)
- category: Sedatives & Hypnotics
- schedule: Rx-only — not a controlled substance; one of the MOST dangerous common drugs in overdose
- appearance: Small round tablets 10–150 mg; also used in low doses for nerve pain and migraine prevention
- effects: Tricyclic antidepressant — heavy sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision (anticholinergic load); At low doses (10–25 mg) prescribed for nerve pain, migraines and IBS rather than depression; Generic and extremely cheap — prescribed for decades
- risks: NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX: a few pills above a prescription dose can kill — tricyclic overdose causes fatal heart arrhythmias and is a leading toxicology fatality; A single adult-strength tablet can be lethal to a small child — keep locked away; Mixing with alcohol, benzos or opioids multiplies sedation and breathing risk; MAOIs and tramadol push serotonin danger; In overdose it paradoxically causes agitation, seizures and hallucinations BEFORE coma
- overdoseSigns: Fast then irregular heartbeat, seizures, hallucinations, hot dry skin, dilated pupils, then coma; ANY suspected tricyclic overdose is a call-911-now event — do not wait for symptoms
- streetPrice: Pennies per tablet generic; no real street market — the danger is accidental and impulsive overdose
- legalStatus: Rx-only; not controlled
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA, PubMed, Poison control guidance

## Clonidine (Catapres)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/clonidine/
- aliases: Catapres, Kapvay, Clonodine (misspelling), The withdrawal pill
- category: Sedatives & Hypnotics
- schedule: Rx-only — not a controlled substance
- appearance: 0.1–0.3 mg tablets; weekly patches; liquid for ADHD
- effects: Alpha-2 agonist — lowers blood pressure and heart rate, sedates, and blunts the adrenaline surge of opioid, alcohol and benzo withdrawal; Prescribed for ADHD, blood pressure, hot flashes — and widely used off-label for withdrawal management; Same α2 mechanism as the street adulterant medetomidine (the 'tranq successor') at a therapeutic dose
- risks: Abuse as an opioid potentiator: some users take it to boost or stretch an opioid supply — dangerous, and it does not produce a real high; Sudden stopping after regular use triggers REBOUND HYPERTENSION — blood pressure spikes that can cause stroke; taper, never stop cold; Fainting, falls, and dangerous slowing when mixed with alcohol, benzos or opioids; Patches: heat (fever, heating pad) dumps the whole dose at once
- overdoseSigns: Very slow heart rate, fainting, pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, extreme sedation; Unresponsive or collapsed — call emergency services
- streetPrice: ~$0.25–1 per tablet; diverted in prisons and jails as a sedative
- legalStatus: Rx-only; not federally controlled
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA, CDC, PubMed

## Lofexidine (Lucemyra)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/lofexidine/
- aliases: Lucemyra, Lofexidine, The official detox pill
- category: Sedatives & Hypnotics
- schedule: Rx-only — not a controlled substance
- appearance: 0.18 mg tablets; taken up to 4× daily during withdrawal
- effects: Alpha-2 agonist made specifically for opioid withdrawal — FDA-approved 2018; calms the noradrenaline storm behind agitation, sweating, cramps and insomnia; Reduces withdrawal symptoms; it does NOT treat cravings the way buprenorphine or methadone do; Same family as clonidine but dosed and studied for detox
- risks: Lowers blood pressure and slows the heart — fainting and falls, especially with dehydration from withdrawal vomiting/diarrhea; QT prolongation (heart rhythm) at higher doses — caution with methadone or other QT drugs; Rebound blood-pressure spike if stopped abruptly; treats symptoms, not addiction itself
- overdoseSigns: Fainting, very slow pulse, dizziness on standing, severe drowsiness; Collapse — call emergency services; hospital admission for monitored detox is safer
- streetPrice: ~$10–15 per tablet retail (often cheaper via insurance); no street market
- legalStatus: Rx-only; FDA-approved for opioid withdrawal symptoms
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA, SAMHSA

## Butane & Lighter-Fluid Huffing
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/butane-huffing/
- aliases: Butane, Lighter gas, Butane huffing, Lighter fluid
- category: Hazardous Substances
- schedule: Legal to buy at any corner shop — no age barrier in practice; abuse kills first-timers
- appearance: Lighter-refill cans, aerosol propellant; inhaled straight from nozzle, through a rag, or from a plastic bag
- effects: 30–60 seconds of dizziness, euphoria, muffled hearing and a 'head rush' — then a brutal headache; Higher doses: slurred speech, hallucinations, blackouts; No safe dose: effects are seconds from dose, so users re-dose constantly in one session
- risks: SUDDEN SNIFFING DEATH: butane sensitizes the heart — a sudden adrenaline jolt (a scare, being caught, even standing up fast) triggers fatal cardiac arrest. It kills first-time experimenters; Frozen lips, mouth and airways from the expanding gas; frostbite inside the throat; Bag-over-head use = suffocation death; vomiting while passed out = aspiration; Chronic use: permanent brain, kidney and liver damage, nerve damage ('huffer's gait')
- overdoseSigns: Cardiac arrest or collapse mid-use — this is often the FIRST sign; Seizures, blue lips, gasping, frozen mouth and chin; Call emergency services immediately; start CPR if not breathing
- streetPrice: ~$2–5 per can — the cheapest high there is, and one of the deadliest
- legalStatus: Legal sale; inhalant abuse prosecuted under public-intoxication/child-endangerment laws in many places
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: NIDA, SAMHSA inhalant guidance

## Flunitrazolam
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/flunitrazolam/
- aliases: FNTZ, Flunitraz, Designer triazolo benzo
- category: Benzodiazepines
- schedule: Unscheduled federally in the US — controlled analog in several states; banned-as-group in others
- appearance: White/off-white powder, pellets and 'Pez' presses; mis-sold as Xanax, bromazolam or 'etizolam'
- effects: Ultra-potent triazolobenzodiazepine — hypnotic, heavy amnesia; active at sub-milligram doses; Stronger per milligram than flubromazolam; more sedative-hypnotic than anxiolytic; Cheap and easy to synthesize, so it keeps reappearing in pressed pills after each ban
- risks: Multi-day blackouts and compulsive redosing — the amnesia hides how much you took; Potency cliff: powder doses are measured in tens of micrograms; a scale error is an overdose; Withdrawal is seizure-and-psychosis territory; dependence forms within weeks of daily use; Fake-pill market: buyers think they are getting Xanax and get a much longer, stronger benzo
- overdoseSigns: Unrousable sleep, vomiting while unconscious, breathing slowed (far worse with opioids or alcohol); Cannot be woken — call emergency services; place on side (recovery position)
- streetPrice: ~$0.50–3 per pressed pellet; powder ~$50–100/g (≈thousands of doses)
- legalStatus: Not federally scheduled (US); several states analogue-controlled; banned in Sweden/Germany/UK PSA
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: CFSRE NPS Discovery, EUDA Early Warning, DEA

## Fluclotizolam
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/fluclotizolam/
- aliases: Fluclotiz, Fluclo, Designer thienodiazepine
- category: Benzodiazepines
- schedule: Unscheduled federally in the US; covered by analogue/state laws and UK PSA
- appearance: White powder and 0.5–1 mg pellets; sold as 'etizolam replacement' after etizolam bans
- effects: Thienotriazolodiazepine (etizolam family) — anxiolytic, sedative, short-to-medium acting; Shows up as the 'etizolam' in grey-market pellets; many buyers have never heard the real name; Lower potency than flunitrazolam but still dosed in fractions of a milligram
- risks: Same class risks as all RC benzos: fast tolerance, blackout redosing, seizure-risk withdrawal; Pellet strength varies wildly between vendors — one batch's '1 mg' is another's 2 mg; Mislabeling: pellets sold as etizolam may contain fluclotizolam, bromazolam or nothing at all; Mixing with opioids or alcohol is the classic fatal combination
- overdoseSigns: Deep unrousable sedation, vomiting while unconscious, slowed breathing; Cannot be woken — recovery position and call emergency services
- streetPrice: ~$1–3 per pellet; powder ~$40–80/g
- legalStatus: Not federally scheduled (US); analogue/state action increasing; UK PSA generic ban covers it
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: CFSRE NPS Discovery, EUDA Early Warning

## THCjd
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/thcjd/
- aliases: THC-JD, Tetrahydrocannabijorol, The next hemp cannabinoid
- category: Cannabinoids
- schedule: Hemp-derived (2018 Farm Bill gray zone) — state bans spreading; no safety testing required
- appearance: Vape cartridges, gummies and distillate sold in smoke shops and online; usually blended with HHC or Delta-8
- effects: Rare natural hemp cannabinoid, produced commercially by converting CBD — marketed as stronger than Delta-8; Real-world evidence is nearly zero: no controlled studies, no standard dose, no verified potency on labels; Users report a heavy, sedative THC-like effect at typical vape doses
- risks: UNKNOWN POTENCY: conversion creates byproducts; labels lie. What one cart does is a guess; No regulation: residual solvents, heavy metals and conversion byproducts have been found in hemp-derived vapes; Same risks as other THC vapes: anxiety, panic, impaired driving; edibles catch people with delayed onset; Drug-test positive — 'hemp legal' does NOT mean test-clean
- overdoseSigns: No lethal overdose known — but panic attacks, vomiting (CHS-style cyclical vomiting with repeated use), and psychosis symptoms in predisposed people; Chest pain from vaping itself — see a doctor
- streetPrice: ~$20–50 per cart; ~$15–40 per gummy pack
- legalStatus: Federally gray (hemp-derived); banned or restricted in an increasing list of states; treated as THC analog by some countries
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA hemp guidance, state regulatory actions

## THCh
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/thch/
- aliases: THC-H, Tetrahydrocannabihexol, Hexyl-THC
- category: Cannabinoids
- schedule: Hemp-derived gray zone — state bans spreading; zero safety data
- appearance: Vape carts, disposables and gummies; almost always blended with HHC, THCP or Delta-8
- effects: Trace hemp cannabinoid with a 6-carbon side chain — theoretically more potent at CB1 than Delta-9, but nobody has published real data; Sellers claim 10–25× potency; users report strong, long, sedating effects at vape doses; Commercial product is CBD-converted distillate — not the natural trace compound
- risks: Potency claims are marketing, not science — overdose-by-cart is a real possibility for naive users; Conversion byproducts and solvent residues; no batch testing required anywhere; Psychosis, panic and cyclical vomiting risk with heavy use — same as any strong THC; Will fail a drug test
- overdoseSigns: No known lethal dose — extreme sedation, panic, vomiting; erratic behavior that gets users medical attention; Persistent vomiting after months of daily use = possible CHS — see a doctor
- streetPrice: ~$25–60 per cart; premium 'blend' disposables $40–80
- legalStatus: Federally gray; several states explicitly banned; several countries treat as THC analog
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA hemp guidance, state regulatory actions

## HHC-O (HHC Acetate)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/hhc-o/
- aliases: HHC-O, HHC-O acetate, Hexahydrocannabinol-O
- category: Cannabinoids
- schedule: Hemp-derived gray zone — state bans spreading
- appearance: Vape carts and disposables; golden distillate, thicker than HHC
- effects: Acetate ester of HHC — sold as 'stronger, slower-onset HHC' in the same way THC-O was sold vs THC; Subjective reports: body-heavy, delayed onset, longer duration than HHC; Another CBD-conversion product; no published safety or potency data
- risks: ACETATE ESTER WARNING: when heated and vaped, acetate esters can produce ketene gas — the same chemistry behind the EVALI/vitamin-E-acetate lung-injury disaster. This is a structural concern, not a rumor; Unregulated potency and purity; blends hide what's actually in the cart; Strong sedation + impaired driving; drug-test positive; No long-term data at all
- overdoseSigns: No known lethal dose — heavy sedation, panic, vomiting; Coughing fits or chest tightness after vaping acetates = stop immediately and see a doctor
- streetPrice: ~$25–55 per cart
- legalStatus: Federally gray; banned in multiple states; treated as THC analog in some countries
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA hemp guidance, EVALI/CDC vaping-injury literature

## Dipyanone
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/dipyanone/
- aliases: Dipyanon, DPP (diphenylpropylamine opioid)
- category: Opioids
- schedule: New psychoactive substance — detected by EUDA; scheduling actions underway
- appearance: White-to-off-white powder and pressed tablets sold online as a 'research chemical'
- effects: Synthetic opioid of the diphenylpropylamine family (methadone's chemical neighborhood) — full mu-agonist pain relief and sedation; Long-acting like methadone: effects stretch many hours and so does the overdose risk; Appeared in EU drug-checking and toxicology as nitazene supplies were scheduled and disrupted
- risks: Unknown-dose powder + long half-life = overdose that arrives slowly and won't let go; Same respiratory-depression kill mechanism as fentanyl; naloxone works but repeat dosing may be needed because dipyanone outlasts one spray; Withdrawal is long and grinding (methadone-like) — detox is harder than short opioids; Sold as everything from 'oxycodone powder' to 'legal heroin' — no label is trustworthy
- overdoseSigns: Slowed/stopped breathing, blue lips, pinpoint pupils, unrousable sleep; Naloxone NOW, call emergency services, repeat naloxone every 2–3 minutes until help arrives
- streetPrice: ~$40–100/g powder online; pressed pills $5–20
- legalStatus: NPS — not approved anywhere; EUDA early-warning notification; scheduling/bans spreading in EU and elsewhere
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: EUDA Early Warning System, UNODC, CFSRE NPS Discovery

## 5-MAPB
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/5-mapb/
- aliases: 5-MAPB, MAPB, Benzofuran ecstasy
- category: Empathogens
- schedule: Controlled analog in many places (benzofuran/MDMA-analog laws); NPS in others
- appearance: Off-white to tan powder, crystals and capsules; sold as 'MDMA' or 'molly' substitute
- effects: Benzofuran empathogen — MDMA-like euphoria, empathy and stimulation; slightly more sedating and 'warmer' than MDMA for many users; Longer duration than MDMA (6–8 hours); Shows up in EU pill/powder testing as a common MDMA substitute
- risks: Serotonin load is real: combining with MAOIs, SSRIs/SNRIs, tramadol or other empathogens risks serotonin syndrome; Hyperthermia and dehydration on the dancefloor — same kill pattern as MDMA; Deaths have involved 5-MAPB mixed with other stimulants or at high doses; purity varies wildly; Next-day crash: low mood, insomnia, brain-fog for 1–2 days
- overdoseSigns: Very high temperature, rigid muscles, racing heart, confusion, seizures; Serotonin syndrome signs: shivering, diarrhea, fever, twitching — emergency now; cool the person, call help
- streetPrice: ~$20–60/g powder; pills/caps $5–15
- legalStatus: Banned as an MDMA/benzofuran analog in UK, US (possible analogue act), Germany and others; NPS-controlled in EU
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: EUDA Early Warning, CFSRE, TripSit/community tox data

## 6-MAPB
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/6-mapb/
- aliases: 6-MAPB, 6-MAPB benzofuran
- category: Empathogens
- schedule: Controlled analog in many places; rare NPS in others
- appearance: White-to-tan powder and pellets; occasionally pressed into pills
- effects: Benzofuran empathogen closely related to 6-APB — entactogenic, stimulant, long duration (6–8h); Often described as smoother but more sedating than MDMA; Appears in EU drug-checking results as an APB/MAPB-family substitute
- risks: Same class dangers: serotonin syndrome in combos, hyperthermia, unknown dose; Very little human data — long-term neurotoxicity unknown, but APB-family compounds are flagged for serotonin and heart strain; Sold under wrong names; some '6-MAPB' is actually 5-MAPB, 6-APB or a cathinone; Harsh comedown and multi-day low mood
- overdoseSigns: Hyperthermia, seizures, extreme hypertension, confusion; Serotonin syndrome pattern — emergency care immediately
- streetPrice: ~$20–60/g; pellets $3–10
- legalStatus: Analog/NPS bans across UK, EU and several US states
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: EUDA Early Warning, CFSRE

## Mitragynine (Kratom's Main Alkaloid)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/mitragynine/
- aliases: Mitragynine, Kratom alkaloid, MG
- category: Opioids
- schedule: Not federally scheduled (US); several states/cities ban kratom and its alkaloids
- appearance: Pure compound: white powder (research chemical). In practice it arrives inside leaf powder, capsules, shots and extracts
- effects: The main active alkaloid of kratom — a partial mu-opioid agonist plus stimulant-like adrenergic activity; Low doses: alertness, sociability (coffee-like); high doses: opioid-like sedation and pain relief; Weaker than 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH), which the body converts it into — but extracts concentrate the conversion
- risks: Dependence and withdrawal are real: daily use builds a habit with opioid-type withdrawal (restless legs, anxiety, cravings); Potentiates other sedatives; dangerous with alcohol, benzos and opioids; Rare but documented liver injury with regular use; contaminated products add salmonella/heavy-metal risk; Extracts and shots deliver many times the leaf dose — see the kratom-extracts profile
- overdoseSigns: Severe nausea/vomiting, sedation, slow breathing (especially combined with other depressants); Seizures have been reported with extracts — call poison control / emergency services
- streetPrice: Pure powder is a research chemical (~$30–80/g); leaf $10–30/oz; the real market is in products
- legalStatus: Kratom alkaloids banned in some US states (AL, AR, IN, RI, VT, WI and cities); Thailand/Myanmar traditional-use rules; several EU countries control kratom
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA, NIDA, DEA 8-factor analysis

## Kratom Shots & Extracts (OPMS-style)
- url: https://plugreports.com/drugs/kratom-extracts/
- aliases: Kratom shot, OPMS, Kratom extract, Kava-bar shots, Liquid kratom
- category: Opioids
- schedule: Follows kratom law — concentrated products are the focus of new state bans and FDA seizure actions
- appearance: Small 'energy-shot' bottles, gummies, concentrated resins and capsules — sold at gas stations, smoke shops and kava bars
- effects: Concentrated mitragynine + 7-OH — several times stronger per swallow than leaf powder; Fast onset (10–20 min liquid): opioid-like warmth, sedation, pain relief; small-dose stimulation in some products; The format driving the poison-center call surge: people drink a whole bottle thinking it's a wellness shot
- risks: DOSE CLIFF: one bottle can equal many grams of leaf — the difference between 'fine' and 'sick' is a sip; Dependence comes fast with extracts; withdrawal is opioid-grade and hits casual users who thought it was 'just a supplement'; 7-OH concentration is the regulatory red line — several states now ban concentrated products specifically; Unlabeled adulteration: some shots have tested with added 7-OH or even synthetic opioids
- overdoseSigns: Severe vomiting then sedation, slow breathing, confusion; Combined with alcohol or benzos it turns respiratory-depression dangerous — naloxone may help in mixed opioid overdoses; call emergency services
- streetPrice: ~$10–20 per shot bottle; extract capsules $15–40/pack
- legalStatus: Kratom-legal states allow leaf but an increasing list (e.g., several 2025–26 state laws) ban or cap concentrated/extract products; FDA has seized imported extract products
- lastUpdated: 2026-09-23
- sources: FDA, state 2025–26 kratom laws, poison-center surveillance
